common_name: White Maman Cochet Rose (Antique White Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant own-root or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun, giving it room to form a full, rounded bush.

directions: White Maman Cochet is a sport of the popular pink Tea rose Maman Cochet, carrying the same large, full, high-centered blooms but opening in creamy white with only a faint blush at the petal base in cool weather. It shares its parent's strong, old-rose fragrance and long, elegant buds that made the Cochet roses prized cut flowers, and it repeats in flushes from spring through fall in warm climates. Like most Tea roses it tolerates heat and humidity better than many modern hybrid teas, shrugging off blackspot pressure that would damage less resilient classes. Prune lightly after each bloom cycle to remove spent wood and encourage the next flush, rather than cutting back hard in winter.
sources: American Rose Society — Tea Rose Class Descriptions

common_name: Climbing Maman Cochet Rose (Vigorous Climbing Sport of Maman Cochet)

planting.note: Plant own-root stock against a sturdy trellis, wall, or fence in spring or fall, and allow several seasons for the canes to reach full climbing size.

directions: A climbing sport of the famous Tea rose Maman Cochet, this variety retains its parent's large, high-centered, soft pink blooms shaded with cream on the petal reverse, but carries them on long, arching canes well suited to covering a fence, pergola, or wall. It flowers heaviest in a strong spring flush with lighter repeat bloom through the rest of the growing season, and tolerates heat and humidity as well as the bush form. Train canes as horizontally as possible along their support to encourage more flowering laterals, since upright training concentrates bloom only at the cane tips. Avoid hard pruning, which removes the older wood that carries most of the flowering side shoots; limit cuts to removing dead, damaged, or crossing canes.
sources: American Rose Society — Tea Rose Class Descriptions

common_name: Souvenir d'un Ami Rose (Antique Rose-Pink Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant own-root stock in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; this mid-19th-century Tea rose performs best in warm climates where Tea roses are grown year-round.

directions: One of the older surviving Tea roses still in cultivation, Souvenir d'un Ami bears large, full, cupped blooms in soft rose-pink shaded with warmer salmon tones toward the center, carried on long stems with the typical nodding habit of the Tea class. Its old-rose fragrance is notably strong for a Tea, and the bush produces repeat flushes of bloom through the growing season in a mild climate. Like other antique Teas, it tolerates heat and humidity far better than many modern roses and asks for little beyond routine light pruning of spent wood after each flush. Give it a full-sun spot with good air movement and well-drained soil, since its large, many-petaled blooms can be slow to shed water after rain.
sources: American Rose Society — Tea Rose Class Descriptions

common_name: Marie Guillot Rose (Antique White Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant own-root stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this 19th-century French Tea rose rewards a warm climate with near-continuous bloom.

directions: Marie Guillot produces long, shapely buds that open into full, double, pure white blooms occasionally touched with a faint lemon tint at the base of the petals, held upright on a well-branched, moderately vigorous bush. It carries the classic Tea rose fragrance and flowers in repeated flushes from spring through fall in warm gardens, making it a dependable source of white cut blooms in old rose collections. The foliage is glossy and holds up reasonably well to summer heat and humidity, typical of the Tea class, though it benefits from good air circulation to minimize fungal spotting. Prune lightly after each flush to shape the bush and remove spent wood, saving any harder renewal pruning for late winter dormancy.
sources: American Rose Society — Tea Rose Class Descriptions

common_name: Bridesmaid Rose (Deep Pink Sport of Catherine Mermet Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant own-root stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this sport of the famous cut-flower Tea rose Catherine Mermet was once grown extensively under glass for the florist trade.

directions: Bridesmaid arose as a deeper pink sport of the celebrated Tea rose Catherine Mermet and shares its parent's long, elegant, high-centered buds, but in a richer, warmer rose-pink rather than the pale lilac-pink of the original. It was widely grown commercially as a greenhouse cut flower in the late 19th and early 20th centuries before fading from the trade, though it persists today in heirloom rose collections. In the garden it forms a tidy, upright bush that reblooms through the growing season and tolerates heat and humidity well, as is typical of Tea roses. Prune lightly after each flush to maintain shape and remove spent wood, and give it a full-sun site with good drainage to keep the foliage healthy.
sources: American Rose Society — Tea Rose Class Descriptions

planting.note: Plant own-root stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; this mid-19th-century French Tea rose is grown today mainly in heirloom and antique rose collections.

directions: Homère bears loosely double, cupped blooms in pale blush-white with a soft rose-pink flush toward the petal edges and center, opening from rounded buds on a compact, twiggy bush. Its fragrance is light but distinctly tea-like, and it flowers in recurring flushes through the growing season in climates mild enough to grow Tea roses outdoors year-round. The bush stays relatively low and bushy compared with many Tea cultivars, making it useful toward the front of a mixed antique rose border. Prune lightly to remove spent blooms and shape the plant after each flush, reserving harder cuts for dormancy in regions with a true winter rest.
sources: American Rose Society — Tea Rose Class Descriptions
